title: Navigating Credit and Debt: Your Guide in Germany
summary: Credit and debt can help you reach goals, but it's important to understand the costs and how it affects your financial future, especially your Schufa score. In Germany, saving is often preferred over borrowing due to high interest rates on debt.

sections.heading: What is Credit and Debt?
sections.body: Credit is money you borrow and promise to pay back later, usually with interest, while debt is the money you owe. Your Girokonto might offer an overdraft (Dispo), allowing you to spend more than you have, but using your Dispo or credit cards can be expensive, costing about 11.5% a year. Informal money lenders charge even more, about 30% a year or higher. In Germany, people traditionally prefer saving over borrowing because debt can be costly, and your ability to get credit is often linked to your Schufa score.

sections.heading: When is Debt Useful (and When Not)?
sections.body: Debt can be useful for big, planned expenses you can't cover immediately, like a Mietkaution for your first flat, which can be up to three months' base rent. However, using expensive credit for everyday spending or things that lose value quickly is generally not recommended. Instead of relying on a Dispo, consider saving for your goals in a Tagesgeld account, which offers about 2.3% interest, or an ETF-Sparplan, which historically averages about 7% a year over the long term. These savings options help your money grow rather than paying high interest on debt.

sections.heading: Managing Debt and Your Schufa Score
sections.body: If you do take on debt, always make sure you can pay it back on time, as missing payments can lead to more fees and negatively impact your Schufa score. Your Schufa score is very important in Germany; it can affect whether you can rent a flat, get a phone contract, or even secure future loans. You can request a free copy of your Schufa data once a year to check for any errors and understand your score. Managing debt responsibly means understanding the costs and how it impacts your financial reputation.

example.title: Lena's Mietkaution Dilemma
example.body: Lena, 22, just found her dream flat in Berlin. The landlord asks for a Mietkaution of €1,500. Lena only has €500 saved and considers using her Girokonto's Dispo to cover the remaining €1,000. However, she remembers that Dispo debt costs about 11.5% a year. Instead, she decides to save aggressively for a few months, putting extra money into her Tagesgeld account which earns about 2.3% interest. She also asks her family if they can help her with a short-term loan, which they agree to, allowing her to avoid expensive bank debt and protect her Schufa score.

takeaway: Understanding the costs and impact of credit and debt, especially on your Schufa score, is key to making smart financial choices in Germany.
